must_find.quote: Promo days sell more than non-promo days, and the gap holds after adjustment. Promo=1 days average 298.4 units (n=104) versus 266.3 for promo=0 (n=626).
must_find.reason: The report states higher promo-day sales with direction, means and a significance test.

must_not_claim.item: sales decline over time.
must_not_claim.quote: Monthly sales means rise across 2023 and 2024, from 219.66 in January 2023 to 324.43 in December 2024.
must_not_claim.reason: The report says sales rise over time, not decline.

must_not_claim.item: temperature is a significant driver of sales.
must_not_claim.quote: Temperature shows no detectable association with sales.
must_not_claim.reason: The report explicitly rejects temperature as a driver.

must_find.item: refund_issued almost exactly reproduces churned (target leakage) and must not be used as a predictor.
must_find.quote: refund_issued is a likely leakage variable:** 95.9% of customers with a refund churned, against 1.6% without. Used alone it predicts churn with 97.5% accuracy. Whether a refund precedes churn is unverified, so this result cannot be treated as predictive performance.
must_find.reason: The report flags refund_issued as near-reproducing churn, as likely leakage, and says it should not be used as a predictor.

must_find.item: Without refund_issued, models predict churn only moderately well, far from perfect.
must_find.quote: logistic regression reaches test ROC AUC 0.612 and accuracy 0.605, against a majority-class baseline of 0.635. Gradient boosting reaches ROC AUC 0.531 and accuracy 0.570, below the baseline.
must_find.reason: The report says that without refund_issued the models are weak, with AUC 0.53-0.61, which is far from perfect, though it calls the performance weak rather than moderate.

must_find.item: Customers with lower usage_hours churn more often.
must_find.quote: churned customers averaged 17.30 hours, against 21.77 for retained customers (difference −4.47 hours, 95% CI −5.64 to −3.30, Welch t p = 1.6e-13
must_find.reason: The report shows churned customers have lower usage hours, with the quartile churn rates falling from 46.6% to 21.2% as usage rises.

must_find.item: Customers with shorter tenure_months churn more often.
must_find.quote: churned customers averaged 29.84 months, against 39.12 for retained customers (difference −9.27 months, 95% CI −11.80 to −6.75, Welch t p = 1.3e-12
must_find.reason: The report shows churned customers have shorter tenure, with churn falling from 49.8% to 24.3% across tenure bins.

must_find.item: The basic plan has a higher churn rate than the other plans.
must_find.quote: Churn was highest on the basic plan (42.8%, 219 of 512), and plus (29.3%) and pro (29.8%) were similar.
must_find.reason: The report states that basic has a higher churn rate than the other plans, with numbers.

must_not_claim.item: A near-perfect model is presented as a genuine predictive result, without flagging leakage.
must_not_claim.quote: These scores are inflated by refund_issued (largest coefficient 3.33; gradient-boosting importance 0.94). They are not a valid estimate of predictive performance while refund timing is unresolved.
must_not_claim.reason: The report flags the near-perfect all-feature models as inflated by leakage and does not present them as genuine results.

must_not_claim.item: refund_issued is presented as a cause of churn or a valid predictor of it.
must_not_claim.quote: Until it is, refund_issued should not be used as a predictor, and its association cannot be read as predictive.
must_not_claim.reason: The report rejects treating refund_issued as a cause or a valid predictor.

caveats.quote: refund_issued is a likely leakage variable
caveats.reason: The report warns about leakage explicitly and lists unverified refund timing as a limitation.

must_find.item: Customers on monthly contracts churn more often than those on annual contracts.
must_find.quote: Monthly-contract customers churned at 37.35% (186 of 498), against 21.19% (64 of 302) for annual contracts.
must_find.reason: The report states monthly contracts churn more than annual, with numbers and significance.

must_find.item: Higher monthly_fee is associated with more churn.
must_find.quote: Median monthly fee is 82.92 for churned versus 63.34 for retained customers (Mann-Whitney p = 4.4e-10, rank-biserial 0.275).
must_find.reason: Churned customers pay higher fees, and the report gives the direction and the statistics.

must_find.item: More support_calls are associated with more churn.
must_find.quote: Median support calls are 2.0 versus 1.0 (p = 8.5e-07, rank-biserial 0.209).
must_find.reason: Churned customers make more support calls, and the report gives the direction and the statistics.

must_find.item: region shows no meaningful association with churn.
must_find.quote: **Region is not significantly associated with churn** (chi-square 2.66, df 3, p = 0.448).
must_find.reason: The report explicitly says region has no significant association with churn.

must_not_claim.item: region is a significant or important predictor of churn.
must_not_claim.quote: Region is not significantly associated with churn** (chi-square 2.66, df 3, p = 0.448). Churn rates range from 27.50% (south) to 34.54% (west), but no pairwise comparison is significant after Bonferroni correction.
must_not_claim.reason: The report says region is not significant and does not claim it as a predictor.

must_not_claim.item: Annual-contract customers churn more often than monthly-contract customers.
must_not_claim.quote: Churn is higher for monthly contracts than for annual contracts.
must_not_claim.reason: The report says monthly contracts churn more, the opposite of the claim.

must_find.item: None of the features is meaningfully associated with outcome.
must_find.quote: Group and numeric features show no significant association with outcome after correction. Outcome rate does not differ by group (chi-square = 3.75, 3 df, p = 0.289), and no numeric feature differs between outcome classes after Holm correction (all five Holm p = 1.0). All effect sizes are negligible (|Cohen's d| ≤ 0.09).
must_find.reason: The report clearly states that no feature or group is significantly associated with outcome, and that effect sizes are negligible.

must_find.item: Predictive models do not meaningfully beat the majority-class baseline.
must_find.quote: The models do not beat the majority-class baseline. Test accuracy is 0.588 for the baseline, 0.550 for logistic regression and 0.531 for gradient boosting.
must_find.reason: The report states directly that neither model beats the majority baseline, and gives accuracy and CV AUC figures near chance.

must_not_claim.item: One of the features (feat_1 to feat_5, or group) significantly predicts or drives outcome, stated as a real effect.
must_not_claim.quote: Feat_3 is the most consistent positive numeric signal in the repeated permutation-importance check, but its effect is small.
must_not_claim.reason: The report mentions feat_3 as a small signal but repeatedly says no feature effect is established, so it does not claim a real driving effect.

must_not_claim.item: A model predicts outcome well, or clearly better than the majority-class baseline.
must_not_claim.quote: Neither model beats the baseline on accuracy or balanced accuracy.
must_not_claim.reason: The report says the models perform near chance and does not claim good predictive performance.

must_find.item: price is strongly right-skewed and has extreme outliers.
must_find.quote: Price is strongly right-skewed. Mean is 289,164, median 217,450, standard deviation 322,321, minimum 44,100 and maximum 4,130,400. Skew is 6.44 and raw kurtosis 59.5.
must_find.reason: The report states strong right skew with skew and kurtosis figures and a very high maximum, and notes the top 1% of rows hold a share of total price.

must_find.item: size_sqm has a strong positive association with price.
must_find.quote: Size is the only feature with a clear, significant link to price. Spearman is 0.887 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.859 to 0.911).
must_find.reason: A strong positive size-price association is stated with the supporting statistics.

must_find.item: age_years has a negative association with price.
must_find.quote: Age has a modest negative association. It is significant on the log scale (p = 0.00029) and in rank correlation (p = 0.00011), but not on the raw linear scale (p = 0.061).
must_find.reason: The report states a negative age association, with its direction and its scale-dependent significance.

must_find.item: rating shows no meaningful association with price.
must_find.quote: Rating shows no significant association with price, before or after adjustment.
must_find.reason: The report states no significant rating association and supports it with Kruskal-Wallis and regression results.

must_not_claim.item: rating is a significant or important predictor of price.
must_not_claim.quote: Rating's Spearman is 0.034 (p = 0.403), and the Kruskal-Wallis result shows no reliable association, so the data do not show that higher ratings raise price.
must_not_claim.reason: The report rejects rating as a significant predictor.

must_not_claim.item: price is treated as a classification target (accuracy, precision or recall reported for it).
must_not_claim.reason: Price is modelled as a regression target with RMSE, MAE and R²; no classification metrics are reported.

caveats.quote: Sample size for outliers: the top 1% comprises 6 rows, so the exclusion analyses rest on very few observations.
caveats.reason: The report treats the top-price outliers as a limitation and runs exclusion and robustness analyses on them.

must_find.item: feat_a has the strongest association with outcome.
must_find.quote: **feat_a is the dominant association with outcome.** Its odds ratio is 3.30 per SD (95% CI 2.76 to 3.95, Holm p = 6.6e-38).
must_find.reason: States feat_a as the dominant, strongest association with a positive OR.

must_find.item: feat_b is associated with outcome, more weakly than feat_a.
must_find.quote: feat_b and feat_d have smaller but significant associations; feat_c has none.** feat_b OR is 1.35 per SD (Holm p = 1.4e-5)
must_find.reason: feat_b is positively associated with outcome and weaker than feat_a, with numbers.

must_find.item: feat_d is associated with outcome.
must_find.quote: feat_d OR is 1.81 per SD on the 850 complete rows (Holm p = 1.2e-13)
must_find.reason: feat_d is significantly positively associated with outcome, with OR given.

must_find.item: feat_c shows no meaningful association with outcome.
must_find.quote: feat_c OR is 1.00 per SD (Holm p = 0.95).
must_find.reason: Reports feat_c as having no association with outcome.

must_find.item: About 15% of feat_d values are missing.
must_find.quote: Missing values: feat_d is missing in 150 rows (15.0%).
must_find.reason: Directly states 15% of feat_d missing.

must_not_claim.item: feat_c is a significant or important predictor of outcome.
must_not_claim.quote: feat_c OR is 1.00 per SD (Holm p = 0.95).
must_not_claim.reason: The report says feat_c has no association, so it does not claim it is a significant predictor.

must_not_claim.item: feat_b is the strongest predictor of outcome.
must_not_claim.quote: feat_a is the dominant association with outcome.
must_not_claim.reason: The report names feat_a as strongest, with feat_b described as smaller, so it does not claim feat_b is strongest.

caveats.quote: **Missingness analysis has limited power.** With 150 missing rows, the eda_2 and stat_4 tests can detect only sizeable effects. The joint model tests observed variables only.
caveats.reason: Missing values are explicitly treated as a limitation with discussion of power and unobserved dependence.

must_find.item: Women survived at a much higher rate than men (about 74% against 19%).
must_find.quote: Females survived at 74.2% versus 18.9% for males (chi-square p = 3.7e-59, Cramér's V = 0.543).
must_find.reason: States female and male survival rates close to the item's 74% vs 19%.

must_find.item: Survival falls with passenger class, highest in first class and lowest in third.
must_find.quote: Survival fell from 63.0% in class 1 to 24.2% in class 3.
must_find.reason: Gives the direction of survival by class, highest in class 1 and lowest in class 3.

must_find.item: Passengers who survived had paid higher fares on average.
must_find.quote: Survivors had a mean Fare of 48.4 against 22.1 for non-survivors
must_find.reason: Survivors paid higher mean fares, with numbers given.

must_find.item: Passengers without a recorded cabin survived less often than those with one.
must_find.quote: Cabin-missing rows survived at 30.0% (n = 687), against 66.7% for Cabin-present rows (n = 204).
must_find.reason: Cabin-missing passengers survived less often than those with a recorded cabin.

must_find.item: Passengers with a missing Age survived less often than those with a recorded Age.
must_find.quote: Age-missing rows survived at 29.4% (n = 177), against 40.6% for Age-present rows (n = 714).
must_find.reason: Age-missing rows survived less often than Age-present rows.

must_find.item: A predictive model is compared with the majority-class baseline (about 62% accuracy) and beats it.
must_find.quote: The best predictive model is logistic regression on the full feature set, with test accuracy 0.855 against a majority-class baseline of 0.615.
must_find.reason: Compares model accuracy with the 0.615 majority-class baseline and says it beats it.

must_find.item: Model results include precision, recall or F1, not only accuracy.
must_find.quote: | Logistic regression | 0.855 | 0.884 | 0.803 | 0.830 |
must_find.reason: The model tables report F1 alongside accuracy and AUC.

must_not_claim.item: Most passengers survived.
must_not_claim.quote: Overall, 38.4% of passengers survived.
must_not_claim.reason: The report says a minority survived and does not claim most did.

must_not_claim.item: Men survived at a higher rate than women.
must_not_claim.quote: Females survived at 74.2% (n = 314); males at 18.9% (n = 577).
must_not_claim.reason: Females are reported as surviving at a higher rate than males, the opposite of the claim.

must_not_claim.item: Third-class passengers survived at a higher rate than first-class passengers.
must_not_claim.reason: First class survived at a higher rate than third class, the opposite of the claim.

must_not_claim.item: Age is the strongest predictor of survival.
must_not_claim.quote: Sex ranks near the top in both logistic regressions (0.579 full, 0.639 brief). Pclass ranks first in both logistic regressions
must_not_claim.reason: Age is not called the strongest predictor; the report names Sex and class as strongest and gives Age as second in the random forest only within-model.

caveats.quote: Cabin is 77.1% missing, Age is 19.9% missing, and Embarked is missing for two rows (the premise of three was wrong). Missingness in Age and Cabin is tied to class and, for Cabin, to survival.
caveats.reason: Missing Cabin is explicitly listed as a data limitation.
